evals.query: Create a Kora ProductController with GET list, GET by id, POST create, PUT update and DELETE routes for products.
expected_behavior: Annotates the class with @Component and @HttpController
Imports @HttpController from io.koraframework.http.server.common.annotation and @HttpRoute/@Path/@Query from io.koraframework.http.common.annotation
Declares each route with @HttpRoute(method = HttpMethod.GET/POST/PUT/DELETE, path = ...), either writing the full path on each route or factoring the shared prefix into @HttpController("/products")
Binds the id with @Path and the JSON body with @Json on both the method and the body parameter
Returns 201 from create via HttpResponseEntity.of(201, HttpHeaders.of("Location", ...), body)
Uses constructor injection only, no field injection
anti_behavior: Imports any ru.tinkoff.kora package
Imports HttpServerResponse or HttpServerResponseException from io.koraframework.http.server.common instead of its .response subpackage
Uses foreign-framework annotations such as @RestController, @GetMapping or @RequestBody

evals.query: In our Kora 2.0 Kotlin service I put the shared prefix on the controller — @HttpController("api/v1") — and every route under it returns 404, but the identical Java controller works. Why?
expected_behavior: Confirms that @HttpController does take a path prefix in Kora 2.0 (String value() default ""), so the approach itself is right
Identifies the cause as the missing leading slash combined with how KSP joins the halves: the Kotlin processor concatenates "$rootPath$path" verbatim, producing api/v1/users instead of /api/v1/users
Contrasts it with the Java processor, which adds a leading slash to both halves and strips a trailing slash from the prefix, which is why the Java twin works
Gives the fix as writing the prefix with a leading slash and no trailing slash: @HttpController("/api/v1")
Suggests reading the registered route template out of the generated <Controller>Module rather than guessing
anti_behavior: Claims @HttpController takes no path argument in Kora 2.0, or that a prefix is unsupported
Tells the user to delete the prefix and repeat it in every @HttpRoute path as the only fix
Blames a missing @Component, a missing @Path binding, or the KSP version
Claims Java and Kotlin compose the prefix identically

evals.query: Our Kora 1.x service has a global interceptor annotated @Tag(HttpServerModule.class) implements HttpServerInterceptor. We migrated to Kora 2.0, everything compiles and the app starts, but the interceptor never runs. Why?
expected_behavior: Identifies the cause as the tag: Kora 2.0 collects server-scoped interceptors by @Tag(HttpServer.class) from io.koraframework.http.server.common
States that HttpServerModule still exists in 2.0 so the old annotation still COMPILES with no error or warning, and the component is silently pruned from the graph
Points at HttpServerModule.publicHttpApiRouter, which declares @Tag(HttpServer.class) All<HttpServerInterceptor> as the collection point
Warns that simply removing the tag does NOT fix it — an untagged @Component interceptor is dropped the same way
Also updates the signature to HttpServerResponse intercept(HttpServerRequest request, InterceptChain chain) with no Context and no CompletionStage
Recommends a test asserting the interceptor's observable effect, because the failure is invisible at build time
anti_behavior: Claims the code does not compile, or that a warning or error is emitted
Says @Tag(HttpServerModule.class) is still correct in Kora 2.0
Suggests removing the tag entirely as the fix
Claims Kora 2.0 allows only one global interceptor
Suggests a foreign-framework registration such as a WebMvcConfigurer or a filter chain

evals.query: Our Kora 1.x application.conf has httpServer { publicApiHttpPort = 9090, privateApiHttpPort = 9095 }. We upgraded to Kora 2.0 and the service starts with no errors, but our load balancer and Prometheus scraper get nothing. What happened?
expected_behavior: Identifies the keys as Kora 1.x names: publicApiHttpPort is now httpServer.port and privateApiHttpPort is now httpServer.system.port
Explains that a stale key is an unrecognised HOCON key, ignored silently, so each server falls back to its own default
States the defaults explicitly: 8080 for the public server and 8085 for the system server
Concludes the service came up green on the WRONG ports (8080/8085 instead of 9090/9095), which is why probes and scrapers hit nothing
Also renames privateApiHttpMetricsPath / privateApiHttpReadinessPath / privateApiHttpLivenessPath to httpServer.system.{metricsPath,readinessPath,livenessPath}
Recommends verifying by actually curling both ports rather than trusting a clean startup
anti_behavior: Claims SystemHttpServerConfig inherits port() = 8080 from HttpServerConfig
Claims both servers bind 8080 and the app fails with 'Address already in use' as the primary symptom
Says the stale keys produce a warning, an error, or a startup failure
Leaves the 1.x key names in the corrected config

evals.query: Set up a Kora 2.0 HTTP server that exposes Prometheus metrics and logs every request, with the metrics endpoint on a separate port.
expected_behavior: Sets httpServer.telemetry.metrics.enabled = true and httpServer.telemetry.logging.enabled = true explicitly
States that both default to false in Kora 2.0, so metrics and request logs do not appear unless enabled
Notes that metrics.enabled defaulted to true in Kora 1.x, so this silently changes behaviour on migration
Puts the metrics endpoint under httpServer.system (default port 8085, default path /metrics)
Plugs UndertowPublicHttpServerModule into the @KoraApp interface and notes it also starts the system server
anti_behavior: Claims httpServer.telemetry.metrics.enabled or logging.enabled default to true in Kora 2.0
Writes an example that claims to demonstrate metrics or logging without enabling them
Uses privateApiHttpPort or privateApiHttpMetricsPath
Claims tracing is enabled by default under httpServer.system (SystemHttpServerTracingConfig overrides it to false)

evals.query: In Kora 2.0 I wrote a custom HttpServerResponseMapper and referenced it with @Mapping(MyMapper.class), but the build fails with 'No component found for dependency: MyMapper'. My colleague has the opposite problem: 'Multiple components match dependency: HttpServerResponseMapper<Order>'. Explain both.
expected_behavior: Explains that @Mapping(X.class) makes the generated module ask the graph for the concrete class X, so X must be @Component even when it has no constructor arguments
States that this is why the first build fails, and that adding @Component to MyMapper fixes it
Explains the second error as two non-default @Component providers matching the same untagged HttpServerResponseMapper<Order> slot
Resolves the second by keeping one provider, or separating them with @Tag, or marking one @DefaultComponent
Notes that the framework's own mappers are @DefaultComponent so a user @Component overrides them without a conflict
Mentions that reading the generated <Controller>Module shows exactly which type the graph is asked for
anti_behavior: Claims the rule depends on whether the mapper has dependencies (that Kora constructs dependency-free mappers itself)
Advises removing @Component from a @Mapping-referenced mapper to fix 'No component found'
Invents a registration API such as a mapper registry or a module method that must be hand-written for every mapper

evals.query: I ported a Kora HttpServerResponseMapper from Java to Kotlin. The Java one compiles; the Kotlin one fails with "'apply' overrides nothing". The signature looks identical.
expected_behavior: Identifies the cause as nullability: the contract is HttpServerResponseMapper<T>.apply(HttpServerRequest, @Nullable T) and Kora's HTTP modules are @NullMarked (JSpecify)
Gives the fix as declaring the parameter nullable: override fun apply(request: HttpServerRequest, result: T?): HttpServerResponse
Notes that the error message never mentions nullability, which is what makes it confusing
Explains that this asymmetry is Kotlin-only — the Java twin compiles because Java does not enforce the annotation
Suggests requireNotNull(result) inside the body when the mapper genuinely needs a non-null value
anti_behavior: Suggests adding a Java nullability annotation such as @Nullable or @field:Nullable in Kotlin
Suggests changing the mapper's type parameter to T? in the implements/`:` clause
Blames the Kotlin or KSP version, or suggests @JvmName / @JvmStatic

evals.query: Migrate this Kora 1.x controller to 2.0: a Java method returning Mono<UserResponse>, a Java method returning CompletionStage<UserResponse>, and a Kotlin `suspend fun getUser(): UserResponse`. They call two services that used to run in parallel.
expected_behavior: States that Kora 2.0 contracts are synchronous and run on virtual threads, so all three become plain synchronous return types
Notes that http-server-common ships no HttpServerResponseMapper for Mono, Flux or CompletionStage, so such a return type fails with 'No component found for dependency'
Notes that the Kotlin processor rejects suspend outright with 'Suspend methods are not supported by the HTTP server controller generator'
Recreates the parallelism with StructuredTaskScope inside a synchronous handler rather than dropping it
Flags StructuredTaskScope as a preview API requiring --enable-preview on javac, Kotlin, tests and the launcher
anti_behavior: Keeps Mono, Flux or CompletionStage as a Kora 2.0 handler return type
Keeps `suspend` on an @HttpRoute method
Suggests adding a reactor or coroutine adapter module to restore the old contracts
Silently serializes the two calls without mentioning that the parallelism was lost

evals.query: Our Kora 1.x interceptor stores a resolved tenant in a Context.Key and the controller reads it with Context.current().get(KEY). Port this to Kora 2.0.
expected_behavior: States that Context was removed from the entire Kora framework in 2.0, not merely renamed or moved
Offers request enrichment as the primary replacement: chain.process(request.toBuilder().header("x-tenant-id", tenant).build()) with the handler binding it via @Header or an HttpServerRequestMapper
Warns to call headerRemove(name) before header(name, value) so a client cannot forge the value
Offers ScopedValue as the alternative for values read deep in the call stack, guarded with isBound() before get()
Mentions Principal / Principal.current() as the purpose-built mechanism when the value is the authenticated caller
Uses the 2.0 interceptor signature intercept(HttpServerRequest, InterceptChain) returning HttpServerResponse
anti_behavior: Imports io.koraframework.common.Context or claims Context simply moved packages
Suggests a ThreadLocal as the recommended replacement
Keeps a Context parameter on the interceptor, request mapper or response mapper signature
Calls ScopedValue.get() without checking isBound()

evals.query: Add centralized exception handling to my Kora 2.0 HTTP service that converts exceptions to JSON error responses for all routes. Here is our 1.x version: it is tagged @Tag(HttpServerModule.class), chains .exceptionally(...), unwraps CompletionException, and calls errorWriter.toByteArrayUnchecked(err) inside try/catch (IOException).
expected_behavior: Implements HttpServerInterceptor from io.koraframework.http.server.common.interceptor and registers it with @Tag(HttpServer.class) and @Component
Replaces .exceptionally(...) with a plain try/catch around chain.process(request), since intercept declares throws Exception
Drops the CompletionException unwrapping as unnecessary in a synchronous call
Returns a caught HttpServerResponseException as-is, noting it implements HttpServerResponse so the handler's status and body are preserved
Calls errorWriter.toByteArray(error) with NO try/catch (IOException), stating that the catch is now a compile error: 'exception IOException is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement'
Builds the body with HttpBody.json(...) and returns HttpServerResponse.of(code, body)
anti_behavior: Keeps @Tag(HttpServerModule.class)
Keeps toByteArrayUnchecked, toStringUnchecked or readUnchecked
Wraps toByteArray in try/catch (IOException)
Keeps CompletionStage, .exceptionally(...) or CompletionException unwrapping
Invents an @ExceptionHandler, @ControllerAdvice or HttpServerExceptionHandler type

evals.query: In Kora 2.0, how do I apply one interceptor to every route, another to just one controller, and a third to a single route? And do interceptors run on the readiness probe?
expected_behavior: Uses @Tag(HttpServer.class) + @Component for the server-scoped interceptor
Uses @InterceptWith(X.class) on the controller class for controller scope and on a single @HttpRoute method for route scope
Describes the order as server -> controller -> method -> handler
States that server-scoped interceptors are sorted by class simple name, not declaration order, and that there is no @Order annotation

Answers the probe question: no — the system server is built by the @SystemApi-tagged factory module, so its router collects @Tag(SystemApi.class) interceptors and never sees a @Tag(HttpServer.class) one; /system/readiness, /system/liveness and /metrics are not intercepted
Notes that Kora 2.0 accepts any number of server-scoped interceptors
anti_behavior: Uses @Tag(HttpServerModule.class) for the server-scoped interceptor
Claims only one global interceptor is allowed
Claims interceptors run in declaration order or that an @Order annotation exists
Claims server-scoped interceptors also protect the system/probe endpoints

evals.query: In a Kora 2.0 controller, what should a DELETE handler return if it produces no body? Does it need a response mapper?
expected_behavior: States that a void (Kotlin Unit) handler needs NO response mapper — the processor emits HttpServerResponse.of(200) directly
Shows returning HttpServerResponse.of(204) when 204 No Content is wanted rather than 200
Warns that in Java the return type must be primitive void, not java.lang.Void, because only void is special-cased
Notes that attaching @Mapping to a void/Unit method re-enables a mapper parameter the generated body never calls, so it only adds a graph dependency
anti_behavior: Claims a void or Unit handler requires its own HttpServerResponseMapper
Suggests HttpServerResponse.noContent() or another fluent builder that does not exist
Returns java.lang.Void as the handler return type

evals.query: I need a Kora 2.0 search endpoint GET /search/{category} that also reads optional page, size and sort query params plus an optional X-Request-Id header.
expected_behavior: Uses @Path for the category segment, with the argument name matching the {category} segment
Uses @Query for page/size/sort and @Header for X-Request-Id, all from io.koraframework.http.common.annotation
Marks the optional Java parameters with org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable and uses boxed types (Integer, not int)
In Kotlin uses a nullable type and no annotation at all
States that there is no required=false attribute; nullability alone controls optionality
Notes that a missing required parameter or an unparseable value becomes a 400 automatically
anti_behavior: Invents a required=false attribute on @Query, @Header or @Cookie
Uses jakarta.annotation.Nullable, javax.annotation.Nullable or @field:Nullable in Kotlin
Uses foreign-framework @RequestParam or @PathVariable
Marks an optional parameter with a Java primitive type

evals.query: What Gradle dependencies, processor and application-graph module do I need to start a Kora 2.0 HTTP server in Java?
expected_behavior: Adds the BOM as platform("io.koraframework:kora-bom:$koraVersion") with koraVersion = 2.0.0.RC2 from plain mavenCentral()
Adds annotationProcessor "io.koraframework:annotation-processors" (Kotlin: ksp "io.koraframework:symbol-processors")
Adds implementation "io.koraframework:http-server-undertow" and io.koraframework:json-common for JSON
Extends UndertowPublicHttpServerModule on the @KoraApp interface and notes it also starts the system server on httpServer.system.port
States Java 25 as the minimum, since Kora 2.0 artifacts are compiled to class-file 69
Does not pin versions on individual io.koraframework artifacts
anti_behavior: Uses the ru.tinkoff.kora:kora-parent BOM or any ru.tinkoff.kora artifact
Uses io.koraframework:json-module (the 2.0 artifact is json-common)
Extends UndertowHttpServerModule, which does not exist in Kora 2.0
Pins 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT, 2.0.0.alpha6 or a 1.x version for a new project
Adds a snapshot repository for a released version

evals.query: I want to build a UserContext object from request headers in a Kora 2.0 controller without parsing them in every handler.
expected_behavior: Implements HttpServerRequestMapper<UserContext> from io.koraframework.http.server.common.request and reads values via request.headers().getFirst(...)
Annotates the mapper @Component, because @Mapping injects the concrete class
Binds the parameter with @Mapping(UserContextRequestMapper.class)
Uses the 2.0 signature apply(HttpServerRequest request) with no Context parameter
Mentions HttpServerResponseMapper + @Mapping for the symmetric response case
anti_behavior: Includes a Context parameter in the mapper signature
Omits @Component on the mapper referenced by @Mapping
Imports HttpServerRequestMapper from io.koraframework.http.server.common instead of its .request subpackage
Uses a foreign-framework argument resolver

evals.query: A security scan of our Kora 2.0 service flags that responses advertise the server software. Another team says the opposite: their monitoring expects a Server header and none arrives. How do the Server, Date and Connection headers work, and can I send my own Server value from a controller?
expected_behavior: States that the Server header is off by default: httpServer.headerServerNameEnabled defaults to false, and when set to true every response carries Server: Kora
States that httpServer.headerServerDateEnabled defaults to true (Date on every response) and httpServer.headerKeepAliveEnabled defaults to false
Explains that the Server value is fixed and a server header set on HttpServerResponse/HttpResponseEntity by a handler or interceptor is dropped by the Undertow transport
Notes the same keys are valid under httpServer.system
anti_behavior: Claims Kora always sends Server: Kora and it cannot be disabled
Invents a key for a custom server name such as serverName or headerServerName = "..."
Suggests adding the Server header from an interceptor as a working way to set it

evals.query: We enabled httpServer.telemetry.logging in Kora 2.0 and set logging.mask = "<hidden>" plus maskHeaders = ["x-api-key"]. The custom mask text never shows up, Authorization is now logged in clear, and at TRACE the JSON request bodies show user passwords. Fix the config and code.
expected_behavior: Explains that there is no mask config key; the replacement comes from a MaskingStrategy component tagged @Tag(HttpServerTelemetry.class), which replaces the module's default ("***")
Explains that maskHeaders replaces the default [authorization, cookie, set-cookie], so the defaults must be listed again alongside x-api-key

Explains that bodies are logged only at TRACE and are masked only when a @Tag(HttpServerTelemetry.class) DataMasker for the body format is in the graph, e.g. JsonDataMasker built from MaskingPathRules.builder().mask("password", new MaskingFull()).build()
Names the format selection by Content-Type: json for */json and *+json, xml for */xml and *+xml, form-urlencoded for application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Links or defers to the shared masking model in kora-aop-logging instead of inventing HTTP-only masking classes
anti_behavior: Keeps telemetry.logging.mask in the config as if it worked
Claims header names in maskHeaders must be lower case to match
Claims Kora masks passwords in logged bodies by default
Uses Spring or Logback-pattern based masking instead of the Kora tagged components

evals.query: Our Kora 2.0 controller reads @Cookie("session") String session, and the value is a base64 token ending with ==. Is the padding preserved, and what about a value with = in the middle?
expected_behavior: States that a run of '=' at the end of a cookie value (base64 padding) is kept as part of the value
States that an '=' followed by more characters still acts as a separator, so values with an inner '=' should be URL-encoded (or base64url without inner '=')
anti_behavior: Claims the parser always strips trailing '=' and tells the user to re-pad the token manually
Invents a config key to change cookie parsing

evals.query: Our Kora 2.0 /metrics scrape is several megabytes of text and Prometheus sends Accept-Encoding: gzip, but the response is never compressed. How do I turn on gzip for the system server, and for the public API?
expected_behavior: States that neither Undertow server (public or system) wires response compression and that HttpServerConfig, SystemHttpServerConfig and UndertowConfig have no key for it
Notes that an invented key such as httpServer.system.compression would be ignored silently as an unknown HOCON key
Recommends compressing at the reverse proxy or ingress
anti_behavior: Invents a compression/gzip config key or an Undertow EncodingHandler hook in Kora
Claims Kora compresses responses by default

evals.query: Kora 2.0 HTTP server: how do I confirm which port the public server actually bound, and which tags does the request-duration metric carry so I can build a per-route error-rate panel?
expected_behavior: Points to the startup log line 'HTTP Server <name> (Undertow) started on port <N> in ...' (also a structured port marker)
Names the timer http.server.request.duration with tags including http.route, http.request.method, http.response.status_code and error.type (plus server.name, server.port, url.scheme, server.address)
Reminds that httpServer.telemetry.metrics.enabled defaults to false
anti_behavior: Claims the server metric tags the route as url.template
Invents a separate config key to log the bound port
